<!-- _class: title -->

# Regression and Prediction

## MBUA 512

---
<!-- _class: section -->

# Regression Analysis
---
```sql-live db=stats_demo layout=rows height=500
WITH d AS (
  SELECT sqm AS x, price_k AS y
  FROM   housing
),
stats AS (
  SELECT AVG(x) AS mx, AVG(y) AS my FROM d
),
sums AS (
  SELECT SUM((d.x - s.mx) * (d.y - s.my)) AS sxy,
         SUM(POW(d.x - s.mx, 2))          AS sxx,
         SUM(POW(d.y - s.my, 2))          AS syy
  FROM   d CROSS JOIN stats s
)
SELECT ROUND(sxy / SQRT(sxx * syy), 3) AS r
FROM   sums;
```

<!-- r in SQL — where we got to -->
<!-- The correlation deck built this query one piece at a time: deviations, their products, their squares, then a square root. This is the finished article, pointed at the housing data the rest of this deck uses. Expect r = 0.939. -->
<!-- Everything that follows turns this single number into a LINE: the slope is r rescaled from SD units into real ones, and the intercept follows from the means. -->

---
<!-- _class: quote -->

"Linear regression is a method that summarizes how the average values of a numerical outcome variable vary over subpopulations defined by linear functions of predictors."

— **Gelman & Hill (2007)**

"Offers a concise summary of the mean of the response variable as a function of the explanatory variable through two parameters: the slope and the intercept."

— **Ramsey & Schafer (2002)**

<!-- Gelman, A., & Hill, J. (2007). Data analysis using regression and multilevel/hierarchical models. Cambridge University Press. Ramsey, F. L., & Schafer, D. W. (2002). The statistical sleuth (2nd ed.). Duxbury Press. -->
---
# Use regression for: Description

![Two groups with different slopes](asset:two-groups.png)

*To see, on average, how much groups differ on an outcome.*
---
# Use regression for: Prediction

![A prediction with a 95% interval](asset:prediction-interval.png)

*To predict, on average, the expected change in the outcome as the predictors change — with an honest range around it.*
---
# Examples

- Predicting the average height of a child from their parents' height
- Looking at the average yield of a crop for a given rainfall and temperature
- Describing the average income of a person, stratified by education, parental income and other socio-economic information

<!-- suggestion: the old deck gave each of these its own slide with a full-bleed Unsplash photograph. They are merged here; split them again if you want the pictures back. -->
---
<!-- _class: section -->

# Regression Basics
---
# Variables in regression

- **Y** = the **response variable** (continuous). Also called the *dependent variable*.
- **X₁, X₂, … Xₙ** = the **predictor** or **explanatory variables** (continuous, discrete or categorical).
---
# Simple regression — one explanatory variable

![Housing price against floor area with a fitted line](asset:simple-regression.png)

*50 properties. price = 80.94 + 3.000 × m², r = 0.939.*
---
# Multiple regression — the line becomes a plane

![Two views of a regression plane over floor area and rooms](asset:multiple-regression-plane.png)

*With two predictors the fit is a plane. With more, it is something we can no longer draw.*

<!-- suggestion: the closed-form SQL we build in this lecture stops being pleasant at two predictors — it needs matrix algebra. Say so out loud: the idea generalises, the hand computation does not. -->
---
```sql-live db=stats_demo layout=rows height=291
SELECT COUNT(*)                   AS readings,
       COUNT(temp_c)              AS with_temperature,
       MIN(temp_c)                AS coldest,
       MAX(temp_c)                AS hottest,
       ROUND(AVG(temp_c), 1)      AS mean_temp
FROM   sensor_readings;
```


<!-- Counting what is actually there -->
<!-- COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(temp_c) counts rows where temp_c is known. -->
<!-- **Run it.** 120 rows, 102 temperatures — the sensor failed 18 times, and every average is over the 102. -->
<!-- *`sensor_readings` is synthetic, made for this example.* -->
<!-- This is the only table in the deck with missing values, and it is synthetic for exactly that reason: none of the real or ported datasets has a single gap, and inventing one would have been dishonest. Worth saying "synthetic" out loud here. -->
---
# Linear regression

The regression of Y on X is:

**yᵢ = β₀ + β₁ · xᵢ + εᵢ**,  for i = 1, …, N

- **β₀** (the intercept) — where the line crosses the Y axis, i.e. the value of Y when X = 0
- **β₁** (the slope) — the increase in Y for a one-unit increase in X
---
# The two numbers a line is made of

![The intercept and the slope marked on the housing fit](asset:beta-anatomy.png)
---
```sql-live db=stats_demo layout=rows height=546
WITH d AS (
  SELECT sqm AS x, price_k AS y FROM housing
),
stats AS (
  SELECT AVG(x) AS mx, AVG(y) AS my,
         STDDEV_SAMP(x) AS sx, STDDEV_SAMP(y) AS sy
  FROM   d
),
sums AS (
  SELECT SUM((d.x - s.mx) * (d.y - s.my)) AS sxy,
         SUM(POW(d.x - s.mx, 2))          AS sxx,
         SUM(POW(d.y - s.my, 2))          AS syy
  FROM   d CROSS JOIN stats s
)
SELECT ROUND(sums.sxy / SQRT(sums.sxx * sums.syy), 3)                                  AS r,
       ROUND((sums.sxy / SQRT(sums.sxx * sums.syy)) * stats.sy / stats.sx, 3)          AS slope
FROM   sums CROSS JOIN stats;
```


<!-- Slope = r × (SD of y) ÷ (SD of x) -->
<!-- Slope: for one more unit of x, how many units of y. It is r, rescaled into real units. -->
<!-- **Run it.** Expect r = 0.939 and slope = **3.000**: each extra square metre is worth about 3 thousand. -->
---
```sql-live db=stats_demo layout=rows height=476
WITH d AS (
  SELECT sqm AS x, price_k AS y FROM housing
),
stats AS (
  SELECT AVG(x) AS mx, AVG(y) AS my FROM d
),
fit AS (
  SELECT 3.000 AS slope, s.mx AS mx, s.my AS my
  FROM   stats s
)
SELECT ROUND(mx, 2)               AS mean_sqm,
       ROUND(my, 2)               AS mean_price,
       ROUND(my - slope * mx, 2)  AS intercept
FROM   fit;
```


<!-- The line passes through the averages -->
<!-- The line always passes through (average x, average y) — that fixes the intercept. -->
<!-- **Run it.** The slope came from the last slide; all this one needs is the two averages. Expect intercept **80.93**. -->
<!-- The slope is a literal here on purpose. It was derived on the previous slide, and re-deriving it would bury this slide's single idea — that once you know the slope, the intercept is forced by the requirement that the line pass through (x̄, ȳ) — under fifteen lines the students have already read. -->
<!-- Note 80.93, not the 80.94 the fuller query gives: the exact slope is 2.99989, and rounding it to 3.000 before computing the intercept moves the answer by a cent. Worth mentioning if a student spots it — it is a real lesson about rounding intermediate values. -->
---
# Fitted values and residuals

![Residuals drawn as vertical gaps to the line](asset:residuals.png)

- **Fitted value:** ŷᵢ = β₀ + β₁ · xᵢ — what the line says
- **Residual:** εᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ — what the line missed
---
```sql-live db=stats_demo layout=rows limit=5 height=414
WITH fit AS (
  SELECT 3.000 AS slope, 80.94 AS intercept
)
SELECT h.sqm,
       h.price_k,
       ROUND(f.intercept + f.slope * h.sqm, 1)              AS predicted,
       ROUND(h.price_k - (f.intercept + f.slope * h.sqm), 1) AS residual
FROM   housing h CROSS JOIN fit f
ORDER  BY residual DESC
LIMIT  10;
```


<!-- Predicted and residual, row by row -->
<!-- Predicted = the line's answer. Residual = what the line missed. -->
<!-- **Change it.** `ORDER BY residual` (no `DESC`) shows the other end — the houses the line most overprices. -->
<!-- The slope and intercept are written as literals here on purpose: the point of this slide is the per-row arithmetic, and re-deriving them inside the query would bury it under five CTEs the students have already seen. -->
---
# Least squares: move the line and watch

![Three lines with their residuals and SSR](asset:wrong-lines.png)

*Move the line anywhere else and the squared misses get bigger.*
---
# SSR — the total of the squared misses

![Residual squares drawn on the housing scatter](asset:ssr-squares.png)

**SSR = Σ εᵢ² = Σ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²**

*The least-squares line is the one that makes this total as small as it can be: 93,044.*
---
# One lowest point

![SSR against candidate slopes, a parabola](asset:ssr-curve.png)

*There is exactly one slope at the bottom — and a formula that finds it without searching.*

<!-- suggestion: the old slide called this "gradient descent", but it was an easeOutCubic animation sliding to the closed-form answer — nothing was being minimised. This is the honest picture: SSR really is a parabola in the slope, and least squares is its minimum. -->
---
```sql-live db=stats_demo layout=rows height=268
WITH fit AS (
  SELECT 3.000 AS slope, 80.94 AS intercept
)
SELECT ROUND(SUM(POW(h.price_k - (f.intercept + f.slope * h.sqm), 2)), 0) AS ssr
FROM   housing h CROSS JOIN fit f;
```


<!-- SSR in SQL -->
<!-- Square every miss, add them up. Least squares makes this as small as it can be. -->
<!-- **Run it.** Expect **93,044** — the same number as on the picture. -->
---
# Is it a good model?

**R² = 1 − SSR / TSS**, where **TSS = Σ (yᵢ − ȳ)²**

R² is the proportion of the total variability that the regression model explains.

*For a simple linear regression, **R² = ρ²**.*
---
# Two roads, one number

![TSS and SSR side by side](asset:r2-ssr-tss.png)
---
```sql-live db=stats_demo layout=rows height=430
WITH fit AS (
  SELECT 3.000 AS slope, 80.94 AS intercept
),
parts AS (
  SELECT SUM(POW(h.price_k - (f.intercept + f.slope * h.sqm), 2)) AS ssr,
         SUM(POW(h.price_k - (SELECT AVG(price_k) FROM housing), 2)) AS sst
  FROM   housing h CROSS JOIN fit f
)
SELECT ROUND(ssr, 0)            AS ssr,
       ROUND(sst, 0)            AS sst,
       ROUND(1 - ssr / sst, 3)  AS r_squared
FROM   parts;
```


<!-- R² in SQL -->
<!-- Two roads, one number: 1 − SSR/SST, and r squared. -->
<!-- **Run it.** Expect SSR 93,044, SST 791,883 and **R² = 0.883** — which is 0.939² exactly. -->
---
# How to win at statistics

![R² and adjusted R² as junk predictors are added](asset:r2-inflation.png)

*Add predictors made of pure noise and R² climbs anyway. Adjusted R² does not fall for it.*

<!-- suggestion: the old slide typed its R² values in — nothing was fitted. These are real fits on real (seeded) noise, which is why R² does not climb smoothly: noise sometimes helps by luck. That IS the lesson. -->
---
# Adjusted R²

**Adj. R² = 1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1) / (n − p − 1)**

- **n** = number of observations
- **p** = number of predictors
- **dF** = n − p − 1 (degrees of freedom)

The adjusted R² accounts for the degrees of freedom and is preferable to R² when comparing models of different sizes.

**Warning:** neither R² nor adjusted R² tells you how well the model will predict a **new** observation.
---
```sql-live db=stats_demo layout=rows height=549
WITH d AS (
  SELECT sqm AS x, price_k AS y
  FROM   housing
  WHERE  is_train = 1
),
stats AS (
  SELECT AVG(x) AS mx, AVG(y) AS my,
         STDDEV_SAMP(x) AS sx, STDDEV_SAMP(y) AS sy FROM d
),
sums AS (
  SELECT SUM((d.x - s.mx) * (d.y - s.my)) AS sxy,
         SUM(POW(d.x - s.mx, 2))          AS sxx,
         SUM(POW(d.y - s.my, 2))          AS syy
  FROM   d CROSS JOIN stats s
)
SELECT ROUND(sxy / SQRT(sxx * syy), 3)                 AS r,
       ROUND(sxy / sxx, 3)                             AS slope
FROM   sums CROSS JOIN stats;
```


<!-- Fit on half the data -->
<!-- Fit on half the data. Keep the other half to check. -->
<!-- **Change it.** Make `is_train = 1` into `is_train = 0` and compare. -->
---
# Reading regression output

```annotated-code lang=r sep=@@@
Call:
lm(formula = price_k ~ sqm, data = train_data)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max
-91.341 -23.642 -10.418  11.539 102.124

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 55.67835   28.23143   1.972   0.0607 .
sqm          3.24252    0.25615  12.658 7.56e-12 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 51.49 on 23 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.8745,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.869
F-statistic: 160.2 on 1 and 23 DF,  p-value: 7.555e-12
@@@
- `Estimate` is the fitted coefficient: this line is price = 55.68 + 3.24 × m². Compare it to the 3.000 we got from all 50 houses — half the data moves the slope.
- `Std. Error` is how much that estimate would wobble if we drew another sample of 25. The slope's is 0.26, so 3.24 is comfortably far from zero.
- `t value` is simply Estimate ÷ Std. Error. Rules of thumb start at about 2.
- `Pr(>|t|)` is the p-value: the chance of a t this large if the true coefficient were zero. For `sqm` it is 7.56e-12 — vanishingly small.
- `***` marks significance at the 0.001 level. The intercept's `.` marks only the 0.1 level: we cannot say confidently what a zero-square-metre house costs, which should not surprise anyone.
- `Residual standard error` is the typical miss, in thousands. 51.49 against prices in the hundreds.
- `Multiple R-squared` is the share of variation explained; `Adjusted R-squared` penalises extra predictors.
- `F-statistic` tests the whole model at once. With one predictor it carries the same news as the slope's t.
```

*Output from **R** — the same fit as the previous slide, on the training half. SQL gives us the coefficients; standard errors and p-values are more pleasant in a statistics package.*
---
# Is it a good model? Bands

- **Confidence bands** reflect the uncertainty about the **regression line** — how well the line itself is determined.
- **Prediction bands** include the uncertainty about a **future observation**, and so are always wider.

**Attention:** these limits rely strongly on the assumption of normally distributed errors with constant variance, and should **not** be used when that assumption is violated.
---
# Confidence and prediction bands

![Confidence and prediction bands on the housing fit](asset:confidence-prediction-bands.png)

*Fitted on the 25 training houses; the held-out 25 are the triangles.*
---
# Heavy metal bands

<!-- _class: quote -->

"At the country-level, the number of heavy metal bands per capita is positively associated with economic output per capita (.71); level of creativity and entrepreneurship..."

— Florida, R. (2014, May 26). *How heavy metal tracks the wealth of nations.* Bloomberg.

🤘
---
# Accuracy of predictions

When we build a model and have a "ground truth", we can measure the quality of our predictions.

![A 2x2 confusion matrix](asset:confusion-matrix.png)
---
# Confusion matrix metrics

- **TPR** (Recall) = TP / (TP + FN) — of the real positives, how many did we find?
- **TNR** (Specificity) = TN / (TN + FP) — of the real negatives, how many did we clear?
- **FNR** = FN / (TP + FN) — the ones we missed
- **FPR** = FP / (TN + FP) — the false alarms
- **Precision** = TP / (TP + FP) — when we say yes, how often are we right?
- **Accuracy** = (TP + TN) / Total
- **Prevalence** = (TP + FN) / Total — how common the thing is to begin with
---
# The chihuahua detector

![100 images classified, with the four metrics](asset:chihuahua-detector.png)

*100 images: 10 chihuahuas, 90 muffins. 72% accurate, 90% recall — and 25% precision.*

<!-- suggestion: the punchline is that accuracy looks respectable while the model is nearly useless. It calls "chihuahua" 36 times and is right 9 times. Inspired by Karen Zack's "Chihuahua or Muffin" (2016); the counts are simulated for illustration. -->
---
<!-- _class: callout -->

# Prediction ≠ Causation

- Causal claims require **no confounders**
- Only valid under special settings (controlled experiments)

Be careful when **predicting the future**, **extrapolating beyond the data**, or **making claims for combinations that are not in the data**.
---
# Chocolate and Nobel prizes

![Chocolate consumption against Nobel laureates per capita](asset:chocolate-nobel.png)

*r = +0.800. Source: Messerli, F.H. (2012), NEJM 367:1562–1564.*
---
```sql-live db=stats_demo layout=rows height=500
WITH d AS (
  SELECT chocolate_kg AS x, nobel_per_10m AS y
  FROM   chocolate_nobel
),
stats AS (
  SELECT AVG(x) AS mx, AVG(y) AS my FROM d
),
sums AS (
  SELECT SUM((d.x - s.mx) * (d.y - s.my)) AS sxy,
         SUM(POW(d.x - s.mx, 2))          AS sxx,
         SUM(POW(d.y - s.my, 2))          AS syy
  FROM   d CROSS JOIN stats s
)
SELECT ROUND(sxy / SQRT(sxx * syy), 3) AS r
FROM   sums;
```


<!-- Check it yourself -->
<!-- A strong r. Now argue about why. -->
<!-- **Run it.** Expect **0.800** — one of the strongest correlations in this entire lecture. -->
<!-- suggestion: a good closing discussion. 23 countries, no mechanism, and an r that beats most of the real relationships we looked at today. What would it take to believe it? -->

/* ============================================================================
   mbua512.css — a MARP theme for MBUA 512
   ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
   An understated, minimalist theme grounded in the visual language of
   Te Herenga Waka — Victoria University of Wellington: a deep bottle green,
   generous whitespace, and a single restrained accent.

   Design intent: quiet by default. Colour and ornament earn their place;
   nothing decorates for its own sake. See STYLE-GUIDE.md for the rationale.

   Usage in a slide deck:
       ---
       marp: true
       theme: mbua512
       paginate: true
       ---

   Register the theme with the MARP CLI:
       marp --theme dev/theme/mbua512.css deck.md -o deck.html
   or add it to .marprc.yml (see the theme README).
============================================================================ */

/* @theme mbua512 */

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   1. Type — imported so the deck renders identically everywhere.

   A single serif carries both display and body: Newsreader, a warm, humanist,
   low-contrast serif chosen as the closest open-licence stand-in for VUW's
   brand serif, Feijoa (Klim Type Foundry). One family throughout means no
   serif/sans clash — the weight and colour do the signposting instead.
   IBM Plex Mono is kept for code, where a monospace is unavoidable.

   Fonts are self-hosted and base64-embedded in fonts/fonts.css (regenerate
   with fonts/build-fonts.sh). This is deliberate: MARP's PDF export via
   headless Chrome does NOT reliably wait for a remote @import, so a webfont
   import gives Newsreader in the browser but a Georgia fallback in the PDF.
   Embedding the woff2 makes HTML and PDF identical and needs no network.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
/* --- self-hosted @font-face blocks, inlined from fonts/fonts.css ---
   (MARP does not resolve a nested @import in a theme, so these are
   embedded directly. Regenerate via fonts/build-fonts.sh, then re-inline
   with fonts/inline-fonts.sh.) */
/* FONTS:BEGIN */
@font-face {
  font-family: 'IBM Plex Mono';
  font-style: normal;
  font-weight: 400;
  font-display: swap;
  src: url(data:font/woff2;base64,) format('woff2');
}
@font-face {
  font-family: 'IBM Plex Mono';
  font-style: normal;
  font-weight: 500;
  font-display: swap;
  src: url(data:font/woff2;base64,) format('woff2');
}
@font-face {
  font-family: 'Newsreader';
  font-style: italic;
  font-weight: 400;
  font-display: swap;
  src: url(data:font/woff2;base64,) format('woff2');
}
@font-face {
  font-family: 'Newsreader';
  font-style: normal;
  font-weight: 400;
  font-display: swap;
  src: url(data:font/woff2;base64,) format('woff2');
}
@font-face {
  font-family: 'Newsreader';
  font-style: normal;
  font-weight: 500;
  font-display: swap;
  src: url(data:font/woff2;base64,) format('woff2');
}
@font-face {
  font-family: 'Newsreader';
  font-style: normal;
  font-weight: 600;
  font-display: swap;
  src: url(data:font/woff2;base64,) format('woff2');
}
/* FONTS:END */

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   2. Tokens — the whole palette and scale in one place. Change these, not the
   rules below. Everything downstream is expressed in terms of these tokens.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
:root {
  /* Brand — VUW bottle green and a supporting range */
  --vuw-green:        #003824;  /* signature deep green — headings, the mark   */
  --vuw-green-mid:    #005c3c;  /* mid green — accents, rules, links           */
  --vuw-green-tint:   #eef2ef;  /* palest green wash — quiet panel backgrounds */

  /* Ink and paper — warm neutrals, never pure black on pure white */
  --ink:              #1c211e;  /* primary text                                */
  --ink-soft:         #5c655f;  /* captions, credits, secondary text           */
  --paper:            #fbfaf7;  /* off-white background — easier on the eye     */
  --cream:            #fef9f0;  /* VUW warm cream — the callout-slide field     */
  --rule:             #d8dcd7;  /* hairlines and borders                       */

  /* Accent — used at most once per slide, for one idea worth emphasising */
  --accent:           #b8552e;  /* burnt sienna — a single warm counterpoint   */

  /* Type — one serif for everything (Feijoa-alike); mono for code only */
  --serif: 'Newsreader', Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif;
  --mono:  'IBM Plex Mono', ui-monospace, monospace;

  /* Scale */
  --measure:          62ch;     /* max line length for readability             */
  --pad:              72px;     /* slide padding                               */
}

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   3. The slide surface
--------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
section {
  font-family: var(--serif);
  font-size: 26px;
  line-height: 1.55;
  color: var(--ink);
  background-color: var(--paper);
  padding: var(--pad);
  letter-spacing: 0;
}

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   4. Headings — the same serif as the body, tight and dark green. Weight and
   size, not a change of family, carry the hierarchy.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
h1, h2, h3, h4 {
  font-family: var(--serif);
  font-weight: 500;
  color: var(--vuw-green);
  line-height: 1.12;
  letter-spacing: -0.01em;
  margin: 0 0 0.5em;
  max-width: var(--measure);
}

h1 { font-size: 1.95em; font-weight: 600; }
h2 { font-size: 1.35em; color: var(--vuw-green-mid); }
h3 { font-size: 1.1em;  color: var(--vuw-green-mid); font-weight: 600; }
h4 { font-size: 1em;    color: var(--ink-soft); font-weight: 600;
     text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 0.08em; }

/* An h1 that opens a slide gets a short green rule beneath it — the only
   standing ornament. Turn it off on a slide with `_class: plain` if unwanted. */
h1::after {
  content: "";
  display: block;
  width: 2.2em;
  height: 3px;
  margin-top: 0.35em;
  background: var(--vuw-green-mid);
}

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   5. Body copy, lists, links
--------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
p, li { max-width: var(--measure); }

ul, ol { padding-left: 1.1em; }
li { margin: 0.3em 0; }
li::marker { color: var(--vuw-green-mid); }

strong { color: var(--vuw-green); font-weight: 600; }
em { font-style: italic; }

a {
  color: var(--vuw-green-mid);
  text-decoration: none;
  border-bottom: 1px solid var(--rule);
}
a:hover { border-bottom-color: var(--vuw-green-mid); }

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   6. Blockquotes — for definitions and the one idea worth setting apart.
   A left rule, not a box. No quotation-mark ornament.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
blockquote {
  margin: 0.8em 0;
  padding: 0.1em 0 0.1em 1.1em;
  border-left: 3px solid var(--vuw-green-mid);
  color: var(--ink);
  font-style: normal;
  max-width: var(--measure);
}
blockquote p { font-size: 1.05em; }

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   7. Code
--------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
code {
  font-family: var(--mono);
  font-size: 0.86em;
  background: var(--vuw-green-tint);
  padding: 0.1em 0.35em;
  border-radius: 3px;
}
pre {
  background: var(--vuw-green-tint);
  border: 1px solid var(--rule);
  border-radius: 6px;
  padding: 0.9em 1.1em;
  font-size: 0.8em;
  line-height: 1.55;
  overflow-x: auto;
}
pre code { background: none; padding: 0; }

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   8. Tables — hairlines only, no zebra fill, no heavy borders.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
table {
  border-collapse: collapse;
  font-size: 0.9em;
  margin: 0.6em 0;
}
th, td {
  text-align: left;
  padding: 0.5em 0.9em;
  border-bottom: 1px solid var(--rule);
}
thead th {
  color: var(--vuw-green);
  border-bottom: 2px solid var(--vuw-green-mid);
  font-weight: 600;
}

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   9. Images — captions and credits pick up the soft-ink colour automatically.
   Emphasise clarity: figures sit on paper, unframed.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
img { border-radius: 2px; }

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   10. Pagination — a small, quiet number. Bottom-right.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
section::after {
  color: var(--ink-soft);
  font-family: var(--serif);
  font-size: 15px;
  font-weight: 500;
  right: var(--pad);
  bottom: 34px;
}

/* ===========================================================================
   11. Slide classes — invoke with `<!-- _class: name -->` on a slide.
=========================================================================== */

/* -- title ----------------------------------------------------------------
   The opening slide: deep green field, the deck title in light serif.
   Minimal by rule (see CLAUDE.md): title and course line only. */
section.title {
  background-color: var(--vuw-green);
  color: var(--paper);
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  justify-content: center;
}
section.title h1 {
  color: var(--paper);
  font-size: 2.7em;
  font-weight: 400;
  max-width: 20ch;
}
section.title h1::after { display: none; }
section.title h2,
section.title h3,
section.title p {
  color: #cfe0d6;
  font-weight: 400;
  font-style: italic;      /* the course line, set apart from the roman title */
  letter-spacing: 0.01em;
}
section.title strong { color: var(--paper); }
section.title::after { color: transparent; }  /* no page number on the title */

/* -- section --------------------------------------------------------------
   A divider between major parts of a lecture. Green field, one line. */
section.section {
  background-color: var(--vuw-green);
  color: var(--paper);
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  justify-content: center;
  background-image: none;
}
section.section h1 {
  color: var(--paper);
  font-size: 2.2em;
  font-weight: 400;
}
section.section h1::after {
  background: var(--accent);
  width: 1.6em;
}
section.section h2,
section.section p { color: #cfe0d6; }

/* -- quote ----------------------------------------------------------------
   A slide given over to a single statement, definition, or question. */
section.quote {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  justify-content: center;
}
section.quote blockquote {
  border-left: none;
  padding: 0;
  font-family: var(--serif);
  font-size: 1.5em;
  line-height: 1.3;
  color: var(--vuw-green);
  max-width: 24ch;
}

/* -- callout ---------------------------------------------------------------
   A slide given over to one short takeaway: dark-green serif on VUW's warm
   cream field. Distinct from `quote` (which is for a cited statement) and from
   `section` (a green divider). Write the message as a single paragraph or a
   short blockquote; both are centred and set large.

       <!-- _class: callout -->

       Databases and analytics knowledge for business
       analysts to function effectively.
*/
section.callout {
  background-color: var(--cream);
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  justify-content: center;
  align-items: flex-start;
  padding-right: 8%;                /* leave a little open field on the right   */
}
section.callout p,
section.callout blockquote {
  font-family: var(--serif);
  font-size: 1.5em;
  line-height: 1.34;
  color: var(--vuw-green);
  max-width: 30ch;                  /* narrow measure; control breaks per line  */
  margin: 0;
  border-left: none;                /* override the default blockquote rule   */
  padding: 0;
  text-wrap: pretty;                /* avoid short orphan lines where it can    */
}
/* A callout may set its own line breaks (one clause/sentence per line). When it
   does, don't also wrap — let the author's breaks stand and the box grow. */
section.callout p:has(br) { max-width: none; }
/* a short green rule above the message — the deck's h1-rule idiom, reused */
section.callout::before {
  content: "";
  display: block;
  width: 2.2em;
  height: 3px;
  margin-bottom: 0.7em;
  background: var(--vuw-green-mid);
}

/* -- plain ----------------------------------------------------------------
   Drop the short green rule under the h1 for a slide that needs a completely
   clean field — e.g. a full-bleed diagram. */
section.plain h1::after { display: none; }

/* -- accent ---------------------------------------------------------------
   Opt in to the sienna accent for one emphasised element on a content slide.
   Apply to a single strong/word by wrapping it, or use for a callout list. */
.accent { color: var(--accent); }

/* -- lead -----------------------------------------------------------------
   A slightly larger opening paragraph for a content slide that needs one. */
section .lead { font-size: 1.12em; color: var(--ink); max-width: var(--measure); }

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   12. Credit line — for Unsplash / image attributions (per CLAUDE.md).
   Use: <p class="credit">Photo by X on Unsplash</p>
--------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
.credit {
  position: absolute;
  bottom: 18px;
  left: var(--pad);
  font-size: 12px;
  color: var(--ink-soft);
  letter-spacing: 0;
  max-width: none;
}
section.title .credit,
section.section .credit { color: #9fb6a8; }


/* ==================================================================
 * WEEK-07 ADDENDUM appended to the course theme above.
 * The platform serves ONE stylesheet per deck (css_asset_hash beats the
 * front-matter css: value), so the theme and this addendum are
 * concatenated. Everything above this banner is mbua512.css verbatim.
 * ================================================================== */

/* MBUA512 week-07 — addendum to the course theme.
 *
 * The look is `mbua512.css`, the course MARP theme, referenced from this
 * deck's front matter (`theme: mbua512` + `css:`). This file is NOT a
 * second theme: it is the small set of rules the course theme does not
 * cover, because the theme was written for MARP decks of prose and this
 * deck is a SQL lecture whose slides carry code blocks and a live query
 * widget the theme has never seen.
 *
 * Everything the theme does provide was deleted rather than restated:
 * the palette, the fonts, the slide classes (`title`, `section`, `quote`,
 * `callout`), their backgrounds and their contrast. The earlier
 * white-on-black reconstruction is gone entirely — including its
 * theme-class contrast fixes, which existed only because that sheet
 * inverted `--deck-ink`; the course theme paints `section.section` and
 * `section.title` with `background-color: var(--vuw-green)` and
 * `color: var(--paper)` itself, so the white-on-white failure cannot
 * recur here. Layout for split slides is the platform's `.deck-split`
 * (§13.24) and is not touched either.
 *
 * Every rule below is here because a check failed without it, and says
 * which.
 */

/* --- 1. Code blocks ------------------------------------------------------ *
 *
 * The theme styles no `pre` or `code` at all — it is a prose theme, and
 * the base slide is 26px/1.55 serif. Left alone, a 12-line query renders
 * at the browser's default monospace size inside that leading and
 * overflowed 12 of 33 slides (up to 528px past the slide on "Quantiles in
 * SQL"). These rules size code to fit a 720px stage and give it the
 * theme's own quiet panel treatment rather than inventing a palette:
 * `--vuw-green-tint` is the theme's "palest green wash — quiet panel
 * backgrounds", and `--ink` / `--rule` are its text and hairline tokens.
 */
.reveal .slides section pre {
  background: var(--vuw-green-tint, #eef2ef);
  border: 1px solid var(--rule, #d8dcd7);
  border-radius: 4px;
  margin: 0 0 0.5em;
  padding: 0.55em 0.75em;
  overflow: auto;
}

.reveal .slides section pre code {
  font-family: "SFMono-Regular", Menlo, Consolas, monospace;
  /* 0.5em of the theme's 26px = 13px, which fits the longest query in the
     deck (the four-dataset skewness CTE) inside one slide. */
  font-size: 0.5em;
  line-height: 1.4;
  color: var(--ink, #1c211e);
  white-space: pre;
  display: block;
}

.reveal .slides section code {
  font-family: "SFMono-Regular", Menlo, Consolas, monospace;
  font-size: 0.8em;
  background: var(--vuw-green-tint, #eef2ef);
  padding: 0.08em 0.28em;
  border-radius: 3px;
}

/* --- 2. Body density on content-heavy slides ----------------------------- *
 *
 * The theme's 26px/1.55 is right for a slide holding one idea; this deck
 * has bullet slides that also carry a query. Tightening the leading and
 * the list margins (NOT the font size, which is the theme's voice) is
 * what brings the remaining text-and-code slides inside the stage.
 */
.reveal .slides section ul,
.reveal .slides section ol {
  margin: 0 0 0.45em 1.05em;
  line-height: 1.35;
}

.reveal .slides section li {
  margin-bottom: 0.12em;
}

.reveal .slides section p {
  line-height: 1.35;
  margin: 0 0 0.45em;
}

/* --- 3. Tables ----------------------------------------------------------- *
 *
 * One slide reproduces the fulmar worked table. The theme has no table
 * rules, so it renders at full body size and runs off the slide.
 */
.reveal .slides section table {
  border-collapse: collapse;
  font-size: 0.6em;
  margin: 0 0 0.5em;
}

.reveal .slides section th,
.reveal .slides section td {
  border: 1px solid var(--rule, #d8dcd7);
  padding: 0.25em 0.5em;
  text-align: left;
}

/* --- 4. Two figures stacked in one column -------------------------------- *
 *
 * The platform bounds a split-right figure at `--deck-stage-h * 0.42`
 * (302px of a 720px stage), which is right for ONE figure beside the
 * text. Two slides stack a PAIR in column 2, and 302 + 32 (the wrapper's
 * row-gap) + 302 overruns the wrapper — measured by verify-deck-split.js
 * as 149px and 190px past the slide, with the lower figure painting over
 * the floor. Bounding the pair at 0.23 (measured: 0.30 and 0.25 still overflowed under the course theme, whose larger type leaves less wrapper) is the fix, and it
 * is expressed as a fraction of the stage exactly as the platform's own
 * bound is, so it holds at every window size.
 *
 * NOT a platform bug: 0.42 is correct for its case, and stacking a pair
 * is this deck choosing a denser layout than the default. If two-figure
 * columns become common, `.deck-split` gaining its own pair rule would be
 * the platform-side home for it.
 *
 * Selector note: nested `:has()` inside `:has()` is INVALID in the
 * Chromium the pod runs (every `:has(... :has(...))` form I tried threw
 * "not a valid selector", which silently drops the whole rule). So the
 * second figure is selected directly with a sibling combinator — no
 * nesting — and the pair is sized by targeting both members.
 */
/* Both members of the pair. Verified against the live DOM: on a
 * two-figure slide `~ p:has(> img:only-child)` selects the SECOND (1 hit)
 * and `:not(:last-of-type)` the FIRST (1 hit); together they are the pair,
 * and on a ONE-figure slide the `~` matches nothing and
 * `:not(:last-of-type)` matches nothing either (the lone figure IS the
 * last), so a single figure keeps the platform's full 0.42 bound. */
/* (week-07 stacked-pair rule removed for this deck: every split figure here is
   followed by a source paragraph, so `:not(:last-of-type)` would match each
   lone figure and shrink it to 0.23 of the stage.) */

/* --- 5. Heading and padding density on code slides ----------------------- *
 *
 * The theme's h1 is 78px tall at y=73 (its `--pad` is generous, which is
 * right for a prose slide holding one idea). On a slide that also carries
 * a query that leaves 581px of wrapper, and five slides overflowed by
 * 32-282px. Trimming the h1's size and the slide's vertical padding —
 * only on slides that actually contain code or a widget, so a prose slide
 * keeps the theme's spacing exactly — recovers the room.
 */
.reveal .slides section:has(pre) h1,
.reveal .slides section:has(.deck-widget) h1 {
  font-size: 1.5em;
  margin-bottom: 0.2em;
}

.reveal .slides section:has(pre),
.reveal .slides section:has(.deck-widget) {
  padding-top: calc(var(--pad, 60px) * 0.55);
  padding-bottom: calc(var(--pad, 60px) * 0.45);
}





/* ==================================================================
 * WEEK-09 ADDENDUM — "Correlation & Regression".
 *
 * This deck is mostly (a) a full-width figure under a heading and (b) a
 * tall SQL fence. The base above already handles code slides; these
 * five rules cover what week 09 adds.
 *
 * Rule 1 is copied from the data-graphics deck (source lines). Rules 2-5
 * are new. The week-07 STACKED-PAIR rule is deliberately absent: every
 * figure here is followed by a source or caption paragraph, and that rule
 * shrinks any figure that is not the last paragraph to 0.23 of the stage
 * (the trap recorded in memory `data-graphics-deck`).
 * ================================================================== */

/* 1. Source and caption lines. Written as an italic-only paragraph
 *    (`*Source: …*` / `*r = 0.967.*`). Small, soft, and NOT italic when
 *    rendered — the asterisks are the hook, not the intent. */
.reveal .slides section p > em:only-child {
  display: block;
  font-size: 13px;
  line-height: 1.3;
  color: var(--ink-soft, #5d655f);
  font-style: normal;
  max-width: none;
  margin: 0.3em 0 0;
}

/* 2. Full-width figures. The platform bounds an image at 0.78 of the
 *    stage (561px); with this theme's padding, an h1 and a source line
 *    that overruns a 720px stage. 0.60 fits a figure + heading + source
 *    line; 0.44 when a bullet list shares the slide. Every figure in this
 *    deck is 16:9-ish, so height is the binding dimension. */
.reveal .slides section:not(.split-right) p:has(> img:only-child) > img {
  max-height: calc(var(--deck-stage-h, 720px) * 0.60);
  display: block;
  margin: 0 auto;
}
.reveal .slides section:not(.split-right):has(ul) p:has(> img:only-child) > img {
  max-height: calc(var(--deck-stage-h, 720px) * 0.44);
}

/* 3. The five-CTE SQL slides.
 *
 *    MEASURED ON DEV 2026-09-21 (verify-week09-deck.js, 1920x1080): twelve
 *    slides overran the 720px stage — the seven full WITH-chains by 171-206px,
 *    and four shorter queries by 6-32px. The chain is 15-22 lines and it is
 *    the heart of the lecture, so the fix must be to make it FIT, not to cut
 *    it (the plan's fallback of dropping the `corr` CTE would have removed a
 *    teaching step).
 *
 *    The platform names its own knobs for this: `--deck-sql-em` is the
 *    sql-live widget's root size, explicitly "a course stylesheet can retune
 *    it like any other deck variable". 1.3 -> 1.0 takes ~23% off every line of
 *    every query, which is more than the 206px worst case needs, and leaves
 *    the text comfortably readable at lecture distance (26px x 0.62 x 1.0 =
 *    16px logical, scaled up by reveal on any real projector).
 */
/* MEASURED ON DEV 2026-09-21, and the first two attempts were wrong, so the
 * finding is recorded here rather than the fix alone.
 *
 * The sql-live editor rendered at 27.04px — slide-sized — so the seven
 * five-CTE slides overran the 720px stage by 171-206px.
 *
 * Attempt 1 set `--deck-sql-em: 1.0` on `:root`. The computed value DID
 * become 1.0 and nothing moved.
 * Attempt 2 also restated `--deck-widget-em: 0.62`. That computed too, and
 * still nothing moved.
 *
 * The probe explains both. The widget's computed font-size is exactly its
 * parent <pre>'s 20.8px x 1.3 — i.e. `--deck-sql-em` is being read as 1.3,
 * the platform default, NOT the 1.0 on :root, and no rule matching
 * `.deck-widget` sets font-size at all from this sheet's point of view
 * (the live rule scan returned []). A deck stylesheet is served BEFORE the
 * platform's own, so a `:root` custom property here is simply overwritten
 * by the platform's `:root` later in the cascade. Variables set in a deck
 * sheet cannot retune a platform widget, whatever the platform's comments
 * say about "a course stylesheet can retune it".
 *
 * So set the size ON THE ELEMENT, where later-sheet :root values cannot
 * reach, and use a selector specific enough to win: 0.62em of the section's
 * 26px = 16px logical, which reveal scales up on a projector and which fits
 * a 22-line query with its heading and its Run/Change line.
 */
.reveal .slides section .deck-widget.deck-sql {
  font-size: 16px;
}

/* The caption and the result table ride the same root, so pin them in
 * absolute units too rather than letting them inherit a multiple of a size
 * we have just changed. */
.reveal .slides section .deck-widget.deck-sql .deck-sql-caption {
  font-size: 13px;
  line-height: 1.3;
}

/* 3b. The original rule. Seven fences in this deck carry the full
 *    WITH d / stats / sums chain — 15-18 lines — and they are the heart
 *    of the lecture, so they must fit without scrolling. The base already
 *    trims the h1 and the padding on a slide containing a `pre`; this
 *    tightens the code leading the rest of the way. */
.reveal .slides section:has(.deck-widget) pre,
.reveal .slides section:has(.deck-widget) code {
  line-height: 1.25;
}

/* 4. The Run / Change instruction under a query. Written as a bold-led
 *    paragraph ("**Run it.** …"); keep it tight against the fence so it
 *    reads as part of the same unit. */
.reveal .slides section:has(.deck-widget) > p {
  margin-top: 0.35em;
  margin-bottom: 0.2em;
}

/* 5. The annotated `summary(lm)` exhibit is the widest code in the deck
 *    (an R coefficients table, ~74 columns). Shrink it a little so it
 *    does not wrap — a wrapped regression table is unreadable. */
.reveal .slides section:has(.deck-annotated-code) code {
  font-size: 0.78em;
}

/* 6. Let a long query be READ on the slide.
 *
 * MEASURED ON DEV: in `layout=rows` the editor pane came out 203px tall on
 * every SQL slide — the same 203px for a 9-line query and for the 22-line
 * WITH-chain — while an empty results pane took 194px below it. The
 * screenshot of slide 43 showed the query cut off at "sums AS (": the
 * textarea scrolls, but a student reading the slide cannot see the rest, and
 * the whole point of these seven slides is to READ the chain.
 *
 * The editor is `flex: 0 0 auto` in this layout, so it takes its natural
 * height — but the textarea it wraps has `height: 100%` against a pane the
 * grid has already sized. Sizing the textarea by CONTENT instead lets the
 * pane grow, and capping the results pane keeps the total inside `height=`.
 *
 * Wave 2 note: once the data is loaded and results are pinned, the results
 * pane will want more than 130px on the slides that return several rows.
 * Re-measure then rather than assuming these numbers still hold.
 */
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql--rows .deck-sql-editor-scroll {
  flex: 0 0 auto;
  max-height: none;
}

/* The textarea carries a hardcoded `rows="8"` (measured on dev) = 201px, on
 * every SQL slide, whatever the query's length — while the longest chain here
 * needs 480px. `rows` is only a default, so a height in CSS wins.
 *
 * THE BUDGET, measured rather than guessed (probe-w9budget.js, three sizes).
 * On a 720px stage a SQL slide spends:
 *
 *     108px   top offset + h1
 *      44px   the <pre> wrapper's own padding around the widget
 *      35px   a one-line Run/Change paragraph  (70px if it wraps to two)
 *      ~22px  bottom margin
 *
 * which leaves the widget 511px with a one-line note and 476px with a
 * two-line one. Those are the only two `height=` values in the deck, and
 * `build-payload.py` is not what sets them — the author does, from this
 * table. Inside that box the widget spends ~26px on its caption, ~44px on its
 * button row and keeps a results pane; the editor gets the rest.
 *
 * Three earlier attempts failed here and each is worth not repeating:
 * computing `height=` from the query's line count (ignored the 44px <pre>
 * and the note, so every tall slide overran); raising it further (hit the
 * platform's 680px ceiling); and trusting "0 overflow" (the textarea
 * scrolls, so a clipped query still measures as fitting — LOOK at a
 * screenshot).
 */
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql--rows .deck-sql-editor {
  height: calc(var(--w9-editor-lines, 8) * 23.2px + 18px);
  min-height: 0;
  overflow: auto;
}

/* INSTRUCTOR REVIEW 2026-09-22: the data slides lost their h1 and their
 * "Run it." note — the query and its result are the whole slide now, and the
 * glosses moved to the speaker notes. So the budget changed completely: with
 * no heading and no paragraph the widget has ~636px of the stage.
 *
 * `height=` is now sized PER QUERY (build: editor + 44 button row + 24 pad +
 * 150 results), and each height maps to the editor line count below, so every
 * query is fully visible with real room for its result. Generated from the
 * deck, not hand-written — regenerate both together if a query changes length.
 */
/* PINNED RESULTS, measured on dev 2026-09-22 after the data load.
 *
 * `Pin result` does NOT grow the widget — it renders the rows as a separate
 * <table> SIBLING below it. Measured: 40px of header plus ~32.3px per row, so
 * a 10-row pin is 363px and a one-row pin is 67px. That is what pushed eight
 * slides off the stage on the first pin pass while every widget still
 * reported exactly its requested height.
 *
 * Pinning is not optional: students never execute a query, so "a pinned table
 * is the only data their browser ever has" (deck help). A slide with no pin
 * shows them SQL and nothing else.
 *
 * So the budget is solved backwards from what sits under the widget:
 *
 *     widget <= 720 - 40 (top) - 44 (<pre> padding) - table - 14 (margin)
 *
 * which leaves 259px when ten rows are pinned and 555px when one is. Ten rows
 * did not fit, so the row-listing slides carry `limit=5`: five rows still show
 * the shape of the data and halve the table. Every query in the deck is now
 * fully visible, including the 18-line train/test chain.
 *
 * Heights are generated from the deck (one per line count, kept distinct so
 * these attribute selectors cannot collide). Regenerate both together if a
 * query changes length.
 */
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql[style*="268px"] { --w9-editor-lines: 5; }
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql[style*="274px"] { --w9-editor-lines: 4; }
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql[style*="291px"] { --w9-editor-lines: 6; }
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql[style*="298px"] { --w9-editor-lines: 5; }
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql[style*="337px"] { --w9-editor-lines: 8; }
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql[style*="344px"] { --w9-editor-lines: 7; }
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql[style*="360px"] { --w9-editor-lines: 9; }
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql[style*="407px"] { --w9-editor-lines: 11; }
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql[style*="414px"] { --w9-editor-lines: 10; }
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql[style*="420px"] { --w9-editor-lines: 11; }
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql[style*="430px"] { --w9-editor-lines: 12; }
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql[style*="476px"] { --w9-editor-lines: 14; }
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql[style*="500px"] { --w9-editor-lines: 15; }
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql[style*="523px"] { --w9-editor-lines: 16; }
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql[style*="546px"] { --w9-editor-lines: 17; }
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql[style*="549px"] { --w9-editor-lines: 18; }

/* The tables are LOADED on dev now and every query returns rows, so the
 * results pane needs real room rather than the 130px that was enough for an
 * empty "Press Run" placeholder. 150px shows a one-row answer with its header
 * comfortably and several rows of a LIMIT 10 with a scroll. */
.reveal .slides section .deck-sql--rows .deck-sql-results-pane {
  max-height: 150px;
}
